claim: Four macaque monkeys (Macaca mulatta) participated in this study.
source: Four macaque monkeys (Macaca mulatta) participated in this study.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the number and species of subjects in the study.

claim: Two animals performed the task in the MRI scanner.
source: Two animals performed this task in a 3T horizontal bore MRI scanner.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental setup for two of the animals.

claim: Two other animals were each implanted with 1024 electrodes in the visual cortex.
source: Two other monkeys were each implanted with 1024 electrodes in the visual cortex (V1, V4).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the electrophysiology setup for the other two animals.

claim: pRFs derived from BOLD-fMRI were most similar to MUA-pRFs in V1 and V4.
source: We found that pRFs derived from BOLD-fMRI were most similar to MUA-pRFs in V1 and V4, while pRFs based on LFP gamma power also gave a good approximation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data presented in the results.

claim: pRFs based on LFP gamma power gave a good approximation to BOLD-fMRI pRFs.
source: We found that pRFs derived from BOLD-fMRI were most similar to MUA-pRFs in V1 and V4, while pRFs based on LFP gamma power also gave a good approximation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data presented in the results.

claim: fMRI-based pRFs reliably reflect neuronal receptive field properties in the primate brain.
source: fMRI-based pRFs thus reliably reflect neuronal receptive field properties in the primate brain.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of fMRI and electrophysiology data.

claim: Whole-brain fMRI measurements revealed retinotopic tuning in many cortical and subcortical areas.
source: In addition to our results in V1 and V4, the whole-brain fMRI measurements revealed retinotopic tuning in many other cortical and subcortical areas with a consistent increase in pRF size with increasing eccentricity, as well as a retinotopically specific deactivation of default mode network nodes similar to previous observations in humans.
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI data analysis presented in the results.

claim: pRF size increases consistently with increasing eccentricity across cortical and subcortical areas.
source: In addition to our results in V1 and V4, the whole-brain fMRI measurements revealed retinotopic tuning in many other cortical and subcortical areas with a consistent increase in pRF size with increasing eccentricity, as well as a retinotopically specific deactivation of default mode network nodes similar to previous observations in humans.
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI data analysis presented in the results.

claim: Retinotopically specific deactivation of default mode network nodes was observed, similar to previous observations in humans.
source: In addition to our results in V1 and V4, the whole-brain fMRI measurements revealed retinotopic tuning in many other cortical and subcortical areas with a consistent increase in pRF size with increasing eccentricity, as well as a retinotopically specific deactivation of default mode network nodes similar to previous observations in humans.
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI data analysis that is compared to previous human studies.

claim: The concept of a receptive field is crucial for understanding the mechanisms underlying perception, cognition, and action.
source: The concept of a receptive field (RF) is crucial for our understanding of the mechanisms underlying perception, cognition, and action.
evidence: This is a statement about the importance of the RF concept in neuroscience.

claim: RFs typically describe stimulus locations that evoke or modulate neuronal responses.
source: RFs (Hartline, 1938; Sherrington, 1906) typically describe stimulus locations that evoke or modulate neuronal responses, but they can be generalized to different stimulus features such as color or spatial frequency.
evidence: This is a definition of RFs supported by citations to foundational work.

claim: RFs can be generalized to different stimulus features such as color or spatial frequency.
source: RFs (Hartline, 1938; Sherrington, 1906) typically describe stimulus locations that evoke or modulate neuronal responses, but they can be generalized to different stimulus features such as color or spatial frequency.
evidence: This is an extension of the RF concept supported by citations.

claim: RFs are usually measured by determining the neuronal firing rate elicited by visual stimuli.
source: RFs are usually measured by determining the neuronal firing rate elicited by visual stimuli (Hubel and Wiesel, 1998; Hubel and Wiesel, 1968; Hubel and Wiesel, 1959), but they can also be defined based on other neuronal signals such as subthreshold activity (Priebe, 2008), properties of the local field potential (LFP; Victor et al., 1994), or calcium levels that can, for instance, be measured with fluorescent calcium indicators (van Beest et al., 2021; Bonin et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a statement about standard RF measurement methods supported by citations.

claim: RFs can be defined based on subthreshold activity.
source: RFs are usually measured by determining the neuronal firing rate elicited by visual stimuli (Hubel and Wiesel, 1998; Hubel and Wiesel, 1968; Hubel and Wiesel, 1959), but they can also be defined based on other neuronal signals such as subthreshold activity (Priebe, 2008), properties of the local field potential (LFP; Victor et al., 1994), or calcium levels that can, for instance, be measured with fluorescent calcium indicators (van Beest et al., 2021; Bonin et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a statement about alternative RF measurement methods supported by a citation.

claim: RFs can be defined based on properties of the local field potential (LFP).
source: RFs are usually measured by determining the neuronal firing rate elicited by visual stimuli (Hubel and Wiesel, 1998; Hubel and Wiesel, 1968; Hubel and Wiesel, 1959), but they can also be defined based on other neuronal signals such as subthreshold activity (Priebe, 2008), properties of the local field potential (LFP; Victor et al., 1994), or calcium levels that can, for instance, be measured with fluorescent calcium indicators (van Beest et al., 2021; Bonin et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a statement about alternative RF measurement methods supported by a citation.

claim: RFs can be defined based on calcium levels measured with fluorescent calcium indicators.
source: RFs are usually measured by determining the neuronal firing rate elicited by visual stimuli (Hubel and Wiesel, 1998; Hubel and Wiesel, 1968; Hubel and Wiesel, 1959), but they can also be defined based on other neuronal signals such as subthreshold activity (Priebe, 2008), properties of the local field potential (LFP; Victor et al., 1994), or calcium levels that can, for instance, be measured with fluorescent calcium indicators (van Beest et al., 2021; Bonin et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a statement about alternative RF measurement methods supported by citations.

claim: The retinotopic organization of the human brain has been characterized with functional magnetic resonance imaging for decades.
source: The retinotopic organization of the human brain has now been characterized with functional magnetic resonance imaging for decades (Wandell et al., 2007; Wandell and Winawer, 2011).
evidence: This is a statement about the history of fMRI retinotopy research supported by citations.

claim: Early fMRI studies used phase-encoding with 'rotating wedge' and 'expanding or contracting ring' stimuli to identify RF position.
source: Early studies used phase-encoding with 'rotating wedge' and 'expanding or contracting ring' stimuli to identify RF position (Engel, 2012; Engel et al., 1994; Sereno et al., 1995), while later studies increasingly used the 'population receptive field' (pRF) method that estimates RF size in addition to position (Dumoulin and Wandell, 2008; Wandell et al., 2007; Wandell and Winawer, 2015; Wandell and Winawer, 2011).
evidence: This is a statement about early fMRI retinotopy methods supported by citations.

claim: Later fMRI studies increasingly used the 'population receptive field' (pRF) method that estimates RF size in addition to position.
source: Early studies used phase-encoding with 'rotating wedge' and 'expanding or contracting ring' stimuli to identify RF position (Engel, 2012; Engel et al., 1994; Sereno et al., 1995), while later studies increasingly used the 'population receptive field' (pRF) method that estimates RF size in addition to position (Dumoulin and Wandell, 2008; Wandell et al., 2007; Wandell and Winawer, 2015; Wandell and Winawer, 2011).
evidence: This is a statement about the development of pRF methods supported by citations.

claim: The pRF method is popular and has been used to map a range of visual and cognitive functions.
source: The method is popular and has been used to map a range of visual and cognitive functions (Binda et al., 2018; Ekman et al., 2020; Harvey et al., 2020; Harvey et al., 2015; He et al., 2019; Hughes et al., 2019; Mo et al., 2018; Poltoratski et al., 2019; Poltoratski and Tong, 2020; Puckett et al., 2020; Shao et al., 2013; Shen et al., 2020; Silson et al., 2018; Stoll et al., 2020; Thomas et al., 2015; Welbourne et al., 2018; Zuiderbaan et al., 2017), dysfunctions (Ahmadi et al., 2020; Alvarez et al., 2020; de Best et al., 2019; Dumoulin and Knapen, 2018; Green et al., 2019; Schwarzkopf et al., 2014), mechanisms of brain development (Dekker et al., 2019), cortical evolution (Keliris et al., 2019; Kolster et al., 2014; Zhu and Vanduffel, 2019), and information transfer across different brain areas (Haak et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about the widespread use of pRF methods supported by numerous citations.

claim: The term 'pRF' assumes that the BOLD signal measured with fMRI reflects the aggregate response of a large population of neurons within a voxel.
source: The term 'pRF' highlights the analogy to neuronal RFs. It assumes that the blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) signal measured with fMRI reflects the aggregate response of a large population of neurons within a voxel.
evidence: This is a statement about the conceptual basis of pRFs.

claim: pRFs of the human visual cortex are qualitatively similar to the RFs of single neurons or multi-unit activity (MUA) in animals.
source: Indeed, pRFs of the human visual cortex are qualitatively similar to the RFs of single neurons or multi-unit activity (MUA) in animals (Dumoulin and Wandell, 2008).
evidence: This is a statement about the similarity between human pRFs and animal RFs supported by a citation.

claim: Most previous comparisons of pRFs and RFs were between species and between studies that used different techniques.
source: However, most of the previous comparisons were between species, and between studies that used different techniques to measure pRFs/RFs (Barlow et al., 1966; Hubel and Wiesel, 1968).
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of previous comparative studies supported by citations.

claim: pRF studies based on intracranial recordings in human patients used a limited number of surface electrodes to measure ECoG or intracranial EEG, but not spiking activity.
source: Exceptions are pRF studies based on intracranial recordings in human patients (Harvey et al., 2013; Winawer et al., 2013), which used a limited number of surface electrodes to measure ECoG or intracranial EEG, but not spiking activity.
evidence: This is a statement about the methods used in human intracranial pRF studies supported by citations.

claim: pRFs derived from the LFP exhibited similar properties to pRFs derived from BOLD signals, including similar spatial summation characteristics.
source: The pRFs derived from the LFP exhibited similar properties to pRFs derived from BOLD signals, including similar spatial summation characteristics (Winawer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about findings from a previous study supported by a citation.

claim: Kolster et al., 2014 compared BOLD-based pRFs in monkeys to the RF properties of single units in published work.
source: Another study compared BOLD-based pRFs in monkeys to the RF properties of single units in published work (Kolster et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about a previous study supported by a citation.

claim: Keliris et al., 2019 found that single-unit RFs in one of their monkeys were smaller than pRFs measured with BOLD.
source: Furthermore, Keliris et al., 2019 found that single-unit RFs in one of their monkeys were smaller than pRFs measured with BOLD and proposed another method to estimate RF sizes.
evidence: This is a statement about findings from a previous study supported by a citation.

claim: Keliris et al., 2019 included MUA but not the LFP in their study.
source: Their study included MUA but not the LFP.
evidence: This is a statement about the methods used in a previous study.

claim: A systematic within-species comparison of pRFs derived from BOLD, MUA, and LFP has never been carried out before this study.
source: A systematic within-species comparison of pRFs derived from BOLD, MUA, and LFP has however never been carried out.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the current study.

claim: The question of what neuronal signal forms the basis of the fMRI-BOLD signal has far-reaching consequences for the interpretation of human neuroimaging results.
source: The question that neuronal signal forms the basis of the fMRI-BOLD signal has far-reaching consequences for the interpretation of human neuroimaging results and is therefore a topic of ongoing debate and rigorous investigation (Arthurs and Boniface, 2002; Bartels et al., 2008; Boynton, 2011; Drew, 2019; Ekstrom, 2010; Goense and Logothetis, 2008; Logothetis, 2010; Logothetis, 2003; Logothetis et al., 2001; Logothetis and Wandell, 2004; Maier et al., 2008; Schölvinck et al., 2010; Sirotin and Das, 2009; Winawer et al., 2013; Winder et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a statement about the importance of understanding the neural basis of BOLD supported by numerous citations.

claim: Some studies reported that properties of the BOLD signal resemble features of both neuronal spiking and the LFP.
source: Some studies reported that properties of the BOLD signal resemble features of both neuronal spiking and the LFP (Mukamel et al., 2005; Nir et al., 2007; Rees et al., 2000), others that they resemble the LFP but not spiking (Bartolo et al., 2011; Maier et al., 2008; Niessing et al., 2005; Viswanathan and Freeman, 2007), and yet others that they resemble spiking rather than the LFP (Lima et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about conflicting findings in the literature supported by citations.

claim: Some studies reported that properties of the BOLD signal resemble the LFP but not spiking.
source: Some studies reported that properties of the BOLD signal resemble features of both neuronal spiking and the LFP (Mukamel et al., 2005; Nir et al., 2007; Rees et al., 2000), others that they resemble the LFP but not spiking (Bartolo et al., 2011; Maier et al., 2008; Niessing et al., 2005; Viswanathan and Freeman, 2007), and yet others that they resemble spiking rather than the LFP (Lima et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about conflicting findings in the literature supported by citations.

claim: Some studies reported that properties of the BOLD signal resemble spiking rather than the LFP.
source: Some studies reported that properties of the BOLD signal resemble features of both neuronal spiking and the LFP (Mukamel et al., 2005; Nir et al., 2007; Rees et al., 2000), others that they resemble the LFP but not spiking (Bartolo et al., 2011; Maier et al., 2008; Niessing et al., 2005; Viswanathan and Freeman, 2007), and yet others that they resemble spiking rather than the LFP (Lima et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about conflicting findings in the literature supported by citations.

claim: All models provided good fits to the BOLD time courses in a range of cortical and subcortical areas known to be involved in visual processing.
source: All models provided good fits to the BOLD time courses in a range of cortical and subcortical areas known to be involved in visual processing.
evidence: This is a statement about the quality of model fits to the fMRI data.

claim: Robust retinotopic information was found in occipital, temporal, and parietal cortex for both monkeys.
source: For both monkeys (M1 and M2), we found robust retinotopic information in occipital, temporal, and parietal cortex (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI data analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: pRFs in all cortical areas with retinotopic information were in the contralateral visual field.
source: pRFs in all these areas were in the contralateral visual field and retinotopic maps were consistent with previous reports (Figure 2B), some of which were more extensive (Arcaro et al., 2011; Arcaro and Livingstone, 2017; Brewer et al., 2002; Janssens et al., 2014; Kolster et al., 2014; Rima et al., 2020; Zhu and Vanduffel, 2019).
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI data analysis shown in Figure 2B and compared to previous studies.

claim: Retinotopic maps were consistent with previous reports.
source: pRFs in all these areas were in the contralateral visual field and retinotopic maps were consistent with previous reports (Figure 2B), some of which were more extensive (Arcaro et al., 2011; Arcaro and Livingstone, 2017; Brewer et al., 2002; Janssens et al., 2014; Kolster et al., 2014; Rima et al., 2020; Zhu and Vanduffel, 2019).
evidence: This is a comparison of the current findings to previous studies supported by citations.

claim: Weaker and sparser retinotopic information was observed in the frontal cortex, including around the arcuate sulcus (area 8, including the frontal eye fields) and in the ventrolateral prefrontal cortex.
source: Weaker and sparser retinotopic information was also observed in the frontal cortex, for example, around the arcuate sulcus (area 8, including the frontal eye fields [FEF]) and in the ventrolateral prefrontal cortex (VLPFC).
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI data analysis.

claim: A voxel inclusion criterion of R2 > 5% was used throughout the study unless otherwise noted.
source: Throughout this study, we will use a voxel inclusion criterion of R2 > 5% unless otherwise noted.
evidence: This is a statement about the data analysis methods.

claim: The relatively low threshold of R2 > 5% reveals retinotopic information in more frontal areas and some subcortical regions.
source: While R2 was generally much higher in visual areas (Figure 2A, bottom panel), this relatively low threshold also reveals retinotopic information in more frontal areas and some subcortical regions (where the signal picked up by surface coils has a lower signal-to-noise ratio [SNR]).
evidence: This is a statement about the rationale for the chosen threshold and its effects on the results.

claim: The functional parcellation of visual areas based on field sign inversions around horizontal and vertical meridians lined up well with a probabilistic atlas.
source: The functional parcellation of visual areas based on field sign inversions around horizontal and vertical meridians lined up well with a probabilistic atlas, co-registered to the individual animal's anatomy (D99, Reveley et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a statement about the validation of the functional parcellation using an anatomical atlas.

claim: R2 values in subcortical areas could differentiate the LGN, pulvinar and some striatal regions from their surrounding areas.
source: Subcortically, we could segregate the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN), pulvinar and some striatal regions from their surrounding areas on the basis of a higher R2.
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI data analysis.

claim: The LGN of both hemispheres in both monkeys contained clear retinotopic maps.
source: In both monkeys, the LGN of both hemispheres contained clear retinotopic maps (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI data analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Retinotopic information was evident in the bilateral pulvinar of M1.
source: Retinotopic information was also evident in the bilateral pulvinar of M1, but some of the pRFs in the pulvinar of M2 were large and crossed the vertical meridian, resulting in noisy polar angle maps (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI data analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Some pRFs in the pulvinar of M2 were large and crossed the vertical meridian, resulting in noisy polar angle maps.
source: Retinotopic information was also evident in the bilateral pulvinar of M1, but some of the pRFs in the pulvinar of M2 were large and crossed the vertical meridian, resulting in noisy polar angle maps (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI data analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Striatal retinotopy was less pronounced in M1 and more variable in terms of polar angle maps.
source: Striatal retinotopy was less pronounced in M1 and even more variable in terms of polar angle maps (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI data analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The CSS model outperformed the P-LIN model in terms of cross-validated R2 values.
source: A comparison of model performance pooled over subjects and voxels confirmed that there were significant differences across models, with the CSS model outperforming the P-LIN model (Kruskal–Wallis test on all four models, H = 21.33, df = 3, p<0.0001; post-hoc Tukey's HSD multiple comparisons of mean rank, R2CSS > R2P-LIN, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical comparison of model performance.

claim: The CSS model fit was better than that of P-LIN in all ROIs in M1 and in 38 out of 39 ROIs in M2.
source: Indeed, the CSS model fit was better than that of P-LIN in all ROIs in M1 and in 38 out of 39 ROIs in M2 (Wilcoxon signed-rank, p<0.05; no difference in premotor area F7 in M2) (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical comparison of model performance shown in Figure 4.

claim: The advantage of the CSS model over the P-LIN model generally increased in higher visual areas.
source: The advantage of the CSS model over the P-LIN model generally increased in higher visual areas (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the comparison of model performance shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The static nonlinearity parameter (pRF exponent) was in the range of 0.2–0.4 and significantly below 1 in all areas.
source: The static nonlinearity parameter, or 'pRF exponent' that models the nonlinearity of spatial summation (Materials and methods: Equation 4), was in the range of 0.2–0.4 and significantly below 1 in all areas (Wilcoxon signed-rank, one-tailed, all ROIs with more than four voxels R2 > 5%, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of the CSS model parameters.

claim: pRF exponent values in the range of 0.2–0.4 represent subadditive (compressive) spatial summation.
source: These values of the pRF exponent represent subadditive (compressive) spatial summation, in accordance with observations in the human visual cortex (Kay et al., 2013; Winawer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the pRF exponent values supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The pRF exponent in early visual cortex is comparable to previously reported values for human V1.
source: The pRF exponent in early visual cortex is comparable to previously reported values for human V1.
evidence: This is a comparison of the current findings to previous human studies.

claim: The exponent value in higher visual areas was similar to that in early visual cortex of the two monkeys.
source: The exponent value in higher visual areas was similar to that in early visual cortex of the two monkeys, and higher than previously observed in human extrastriate cortex, which suggests that spatial suppression is less pronounced in higher areas of the monkey visual cortex than in higher areas of the human visual cortex.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of the CSS model parameters and a comparison to human data.

claim: Both the U-LIN model and the DoG model performed better than the standard P-LIN model.
source: Both the U-LIN model and the DoG model also performed better than the standard P-LIN model (Kruskal–Wallis, Tukey's HSD, both ps<0.0001).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical comparison of model performance.

claim: The DoG model had slightly better fits across all pooled voxels than the U-LIN model.
source: The DoG had slightly better fits across all pooled voxels than the U-LIN model (Kruskal–Wallis, Tukey's HSD, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical comparison of model performance.

claim: The advantage of the DoG model over the P-LIN model was most pronounced in V1 and decreased in higher visual areas.
source: The advantage of the DoG model over the P-LIN model was most pronounced in V1 and decreased in higher visual areas.
evidence: This is a finding from the comparison of model performance across brain areas.

claim: There was a subset of voxels with negative BOLD responses for which both the U-LIN and DoG models provided much better pRF fits than the P-LIN and CSS models.
source: There was a subset of voxels with negative BOLD responses for which both the U-LIN and DoG models provided much better pRF fits than the P-LIN and CSS models (arrows in Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from the comparison of model performance shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The U-LIN model estimated a negative gain for voxels where R2 in the U-LIN/DOG models was at least 5% higher than in the P-LIN model.
source: We inspected the voxels for which the R2 in the U-LIN/DOG models was at least 5% higher than in the P-LIN model (gray, dashed triangles in Figure 4A). The U-LIN model estimated a negative gain for these voxels (median gain = –0.31, Wilcoxon signed-rank, one-tailed, z = –43.9, p<0.0001) (Figure 4B) and the DoG model returned a high level of inhibition (median normalized suppressive amplitude = 1.14, interquartile range [IQR], 0.98–1.29).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of voxels with negative BOLD responses shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: The DoG model returned a high level of inhibition for voxels where R2 in the U-LIN/DOG models was at least 5% higher than in the P-LIN model.
source: We inspected the voxels for which the R2 in the U-LIN/DOG models was at least 5% higher than in the P-LIN model (gray, dashed triangles in Figure 4A). The U-LIN model estimated a negative gain for these voxels (median gain = –0.31, Wilcoxon signed-rank, one-tailed, z = –43.9, p<0.0001) (Figure 4B) and the DoG model returned a high level of inhibition (median normalized suppressive amplitude = 1.14, interquartile range [IQR], 0.98–1.29).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of voxels with negative BOLD responses shown in Figure 4A.

claim: There were two categories of voxels with negative responses.
source: There were two categories of voxels with negative responses (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of voxels with negative BOLD responses shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: For the first category of voxels with negative responses, the P-LIN model estimated pRFs outside the boundaries of the stimulated visual field.
source: For the first category of voxels, the P-LIN model estimated pRFs outside the boundaries of the stimulated visual field. This result suggests that the negative response represents surround suppression that is particularly strong around the fovea (Sereno et al., 1995; Shmuel et al., 2006; Smith et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of voxels with negative BOLD responses and an interpretation supported by citations.

claim: The negative response in the first category of voxels represents surround suppression that is particularly strong around the fovea.
source: For the first category of voxels, the P-LIN model estimated pRFs outside the boundaries of the stimulated visual field. This result suggests that the negative response represents surround suppression that is particularly strong around the fovea (Sereno et al., 1995; Shmuel et al., 2006; Smith et al., 2004).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The retinotopy of voxels with negative responses in the first category is consistent with surround suppression around the fovea.
source: The retinotopy of these voxels is consistent with this explanation. In V1, for instance, the voxels were on the medial side of the occipital pole, which represents the peripheral visual field (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of voxels with negative BOLD responses shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The second category of voxels with negative pRFs had purely negative BOLD responses where P-LIN and CSS models could not fit any pRF.
source: The second category of voxels with negative pRFs appeared to be different. Here, P-LIN and CSS models could not fit any pRF, suggesting purely negative BOLD responses.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of voxels with negative BOLD responses.

claim: Voxels with purely negative BOLD responses were primarily located in the medial occipital parietal cortex (mOP), at the superior border of the superior temporal sulcus in the lateral occipital parietal cortex (lOP) and around the lateral sulcus (LatS).
source: These voxels were primarily located in the medial occipital parietal cortex (mOP), at the superior border of the superior temporal sulcus in the lateral occipital parietal cortex (lOP) and around the lateral sulcus (LatS), which includes parts of the insula, cingulate, parietal, and premotor cortices (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of voxels with negative BOLD responses shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Areas with purely negative BOLD responses have all previously been identified as being part of the monkey DMN.
source: These areas have all previously been identified as being part of the monkey DMN (Mantini et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a comparison of the current findings to previous studies supported by a citation.

claim: The finding of negatively tuned pRFs in the monkey DMN aligns with recent research in humans that revealed similar negatively tuned pRFs in corresponding nodes of the human DMN.
source: This finding aligns with recent research in humans that revealed similar negatively tuned pRFs in corresponding nodes of the human DMN (Szinte and Knapen, 2020).
evidence: This is a comparison of the current findings to recent human studies supported by a citation.

claim: pRF sizes were larger at higher eccentricities in all areas with larger numbers of well-fit voxels.
source: As expected, pRF sizes were larger at higher eccentricities. This relationship was evident in all areas with larger numbers of well-fit voxels.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of the relationship between pRF size and eccentricity.

claim: pRFs were larger in higher areas, which exhibited a steeper slope of the eccentricity-size relationship.
source: pRFs were also larger in higher areas, which exhibited a steeper slope of the eccentricity-size relationship (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of the relationship between pRF size and eccentricity shown in Figure 5 and supplements.

claim: The differences between the slopes in V1 and V2 are smaller than expected based on previous electrophysiological studies, but this is not uncommon with fMRI.
source: The differences between the slopes in V1 and V2 are smaller than expected based on previous electrophysiological studies, but this is not uncommon with fMRI (Kay et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a comparison of the current findings to previous studies and an acknowledgment of known fMRI limitations supported by a citation.

claim: Retinotopy was unexpectedly observed in the anterior cingulate cortex in one animal.
source: In one animal, we also unexpectedly observed retinotopy in a number of higher areas, such as the anterior cingulate cortex (Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the fMRI data analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: The anterior cingulate cortex has been studied predominantly in the context of decision-making.
source: This brain region has been studied predominantly in the context of decision-making (Amiez et al., 2006; Fouragnan et al., 2019), but it does have resting state correlations with V1 (Griffis et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a statement about previous research on the anterior cingulate cortex supported by citations.

claim: The anterior cingulate cortex has resting state correlations with V1.
source: This brain region has been studied predominantly in the context of decision-making (Amiez et al., 2006; Fouragnan et al., 2019), but it does have resting state correlations with V1 (Griffis et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a statement about previous research supported by a citation.

claim: Excellent fits to the MUA were obtained for all pRF models.
source: We obtained excellent fits to the MUA for all pRF models (see Figure 1E for an example fit).
evidence: This is a statement about the quality of model fits to the MUA data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: MUA pRFs covered a large proportion of the lower-right visual field.
source: These pRFs covered a large proportion of the lower-right visual field (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the electrophysiology data analysis shown in Figure 6 and supplement.

claim: The locations of pRFs from electrodes of the same arrays were clustered in space and in accordance with established retinotopy.

claim: Cross-validated comparisons revealed significant differences between the four pRF models for MUA data.

claim: The CSS and DoG models provided a better fit than the linear models for MUA data.

claim: The improved fit of the DoG model for MUA was caused by the suppressive surround.

source: The pRF exponent of the CSS model was 0.38 ± 0.23 in V1 (mean ± SD; 1358 electrodes with R2 > 25%), which was significantly smaller than 1 (Wilcoxon signed-rank, one-tailed, z = –31.59, p<0.0001) and similar to the MRI-based values, which had a mean of 0.34 ± 0.19 (6341 voxels).

claim: The pRF exponent of the CSS model for MUA in V1 was similar to the MRI-based values.
source: The pRF exponent of the CSS model was 0.38 ± 0.23 in V1 (mean ± SD; 1358 electrodes with R2 > 25%), which was significantly smaller than 1 (Wilcoxon signed-rank, one-tailed, z = –31.59, p<0.0001) and similar to the MRI-based values, which had a mean of 0.34 ± 0.19 (6341 voxels).
evidence: This is a finding from the comparison of CSS model parameters between MUA and fMRI data.

claim: Negative pRFs generally had lower eccentricities than positive pRFs in the α and β frequency bands.
source: We observed a number of remarkable differences between the positive and negative pRFs. First, negative pRFs generally had lower eccentricities than positive pRFs (Figure 10B, Figure 10—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of positive and negative LFP pRFs shown in Figure 10B and Figure 10—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Negative pRFs were larger than positive pRFs in the α and β frequency bands.
source: Second, negative pRFs were larger than positive pRFs (Figure 10C, Figure 10—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of positive and negative LFP pRFs shown in Figure 10C and Figure 10—figure supplement 1C.

claim: There was a systematic difference in the distance from the γ-pRF of the same electrode between positive and negative pRFs in the α and β frequency bands.
source: Third, there was a systematic difference in the distance from the γ-pRF of the same electrode. A separation index of less than 1 indicates pRF overlap. For both α and β power, the negative pRFs were farther from the γ-pRFs than the positive pRFs (Figure 10D, Figure 10—figure supplement 1D) and generally shifted in the direction of fixation (Figure 10E, Figure 10—figure supplements 1E and 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of positive and negative LFP pRFs shown in Figure 10D, 10E, and supplements.

claim: Negative pRFs in the α and β frequency bands were farther from the γ-pRFs than the positive pRFs.
source: For both α and β power, the negative pRFs were farther from the γ-pRFs than the positive pRFs (Figure 10D, Figure 10—figure supplement 1D) and generally shifted in the direction of fixation (Figure 10E, Figure 10—figure supplements 1E and 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of positive and negative LFP pRFs shown in Figure 10D and Figure 10—figure supplement 1D.

source: For both α and β power, the negative pRFs were farther from the γ-pRFs than the positive pRFs (Figure 10D, Figure 10—figure supplement 1D) and generally shifted in the direction of fixation (Figure 10E, Figure 10—figure supplements 1E and 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of positive and negative LFP pRFs shown in Figure 10E and supplements.

claim: The positive pRFs in the α and β frequency bands represent visually driven activity.
source: These results suggest that the positive pRFs represent visually driven activity, whereas the negative pRFs signal a form of suppression that is strongest at smaller eccentricities, close to the fixation point.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings about positive and negative LFP pRFs.

claim: The negative pRFs in the α and β frequency bands signal a form of suppression that is strongest at smaller eccentricities, close to the fixation point.
source: These results suggest that the positive pRFs represent visually driven activity, whereas the negative pRFs signal a form of suppression that is strongest at smaller eccentricities, close to the fixation point.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings about positive and negative LFP pRFs.

source: One possible explanation is that the monkeys directed attention to the fixation point, which may have caused a ring of suppression closely surrounding it.
evidence: This is a speculation about the cause of negative pRFs in the α and β frequency bands.

source: Another possibility is that the negative pRFs might be a consequence of small eye movements around the fixation point.
evidence: This is a speculation about the cause of negative pRFs in the α and β frequency bands.

claim: All LFP-pRF size estimates were larger than MUA-pRFs.
source: We next analyzed RF sizes, normalizing the size estimates to the MUA-cRF. All LFP-pRFs estimates were larger than MUA-pRFs, and lower frequency LFP components yielded larger pRFs than the higher frequencies (Figure 11B; we observed the same pattern present in each animal).

evidence: This is a finding from the comparison of pRF sizes across electrophysiology signals shown in Figure 11B.

evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of the CSS model parameters for LFP data.

claim: The pRF exponent was smaller at lower LFP frequencies, indicative of stronger CSS.
source: The pRF exponent was well below 1 for all LFP components (V1 and V4 electrodes with R2 > 25%; Wilcoxon signed-rank, one-tailed <1, p<0.001) and smaller at lower frequencies, indicative of stronger CSS.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of the CSS model parameters for LFP data.

claim: The exponent of the MRI was not significantly different from that of γlow in V1.

claim: The exponent of the MRI was not significantly different from that of γlow and γhigh in V4.
source: We also compared the exponents to those of the MRI-pRFs. The exponent of the MRI was not significantly different from that of γlow in V1, and both γlow and γhigh in V4 (p>0.05, Figure 11C).
evidence: This is a finding from the comparison of CSS model parameters between MRI and LFP data shown in Figure 11C.

claim: Differences between the MRI exponent and those of the other LFP bands were significant.
